children.text: Egypt doesn't look like a country of lakes.

From a distance on the map, the eye lands on the Nile. A single line runs south to north, with towns and farmland on each side and desert beyond. For most travellers, Egypt's water seems covered by the Nile, the Red Sea, and the Mediterranean.

The actual Egypt has lakes. Enormous artificial reservoirs, salt lakes surviving from antiquity, desert lakes born of agricultural drainage, shallow lagoons between the Nile Delta and the Mediterranean, lakes built into the corridor of the
Suez
Canal. None of them is enough seen only as a pretty sight.

Egypt's lakes always sit at a boundary. Between desert and water. Between fresh and salt. Between nature and engineering. Between habitat and human drainage and reclamation. Looking there, you see how this country has used water, lost water, and tried to defend it.
Lake Nasser
Egypt's largest lake is not natural.
Lake Nasser is the vast reservoir created by
the Aswan High Dam

. Once the dam was completed across the 1960s and 1970s, the southern stretch of the Nile valley was widely flooded, becoming what is Lake Nasser on the Egyptian side and Lake Nubia on the Sudanese side.
For travellers, Lake Nasser is most often remembered as the quiet water behind
Abu Simbel

. The Great Temple of Ramses II and the smaller temple of Nefertari were not originally where you see them. Because of the dam's flooding, they were moved to higher ground in the 1960s through the UNESCO-led international rescue. Philae was moved to a different island in the same wave.

The lake gave Egypt steady water and electricity. It also relocated Nubian villages and put the old valley landscape under water. So you cannot simply call Lake Nasser "a beautiful lake." A necessary modern Egyptian project, and a place with serious cost.
Going from
Aswan
to Abu Simbel, few travellers target the lake itself. With time, a Lake Nasser cruise is an option. Several days between Aswan and Abu Simbel, visiting Wadi El Sebua, Amada, and
Qasr Ibrim
— southern sites a standard Nile cruise does not reach.

The lake's strength is not display. The surface is wide, the banks are bare desert, and the sense of towns is thin. Unlike the Nile north of Aswan, here the river does not weave life — water fills a large absence.
Lake Qarun
Lake Qarun in Fayoum carries the opposite character. Old, shrinking, growing more saline over time.

In antiquity, a much larger body of water filled the Fayoum depression. Known in Greek as Lake Moeris, it linked to a system that received and returned Nile water, supporting Fayoum's agriculture. The kings of the Twelfth Dynasty treated this depression as a major site for irrigation and water management.

Today's Lake Qarun is a remnant of that ancient lake. With no natural outlet, drainage from surrounding farmland and evaporation have made the salinity high. There is some resort development along its shore; the lake itself is not a simple paradise. It carries problems of water quality, salinity, fishery, and ecology.
It is still worth seeing. Beyond the view, here you see the scale at which Egypt's old water management worked. History read not through stone monuments in
Giza
or
Luxor
but through water level, canals, dykes, fields, and the shrinkage of a lake.

On the west side is the temple of Qasr Qarun. Not a crowded site, but a good stop for going deeper into Fayoum. Rather than aiming at Lake Qarun alone, place it inside Fayoum as a whole alongside Meidum, Hawara, Wadi El Rayan, and Wadi El Hitan.
Wadi El Rayan
Within Fayoum Governorate, Wadi El Rayan is a separate water area from Lake Qarun.

Its two lakes are not ancient. From the 1970s onward, Fayoum's agricultural drainage was guided into the desert depression, and water accumulated over time. The place where water falls between the upper and lower lakes is sometimes introduced as Egypt's only waterfall.

To be strict, imagining a great natural waterfall here would miss it. The water came from irrigation and drainage. Even so, water appearing in desert and falling between low cliffs and sand carries its own force.
Wadi El Rayan fits a day trip from
Cairo

or a Fayoum stay. Nearby Wadi El Hitan is the UNESCO World Heritage Site known for early whale fossils. Seeing water and fossils on the same day, you understand this region not as a "desert view" but as a place with very long geological and water memory.
The Delta lagoons
Along the northern Nile Delta, shallow lagoons line the boundary with the Mediterranean. Lake Manzala, Lake Burullus, Lake Edku, Lake Maryut and others.

These are not lakes travellers casually swim in. Many are fisheries, migratory bird habitats, and at the same time face pressures of agricultural drainage, urban drainage, reclamation, and pollution. Thinking about Egypt's environment, the Delta lagoons cannot be skipped.
Lake Manzala is the large lagoon in the northeastern Delta near
Port Said

. Smaller than it once was and burdened with pollution, it remains important for fisheries and birds. Lake Burullus among the Delta lagoons is known as a protected area, important for winter waterbirds. Lake Edku, near
Alexandria
, is comparatively small. Lake Maryut, tied to ancient Alexandria, was historically linked with wine production and waterways.

Whether to put these on the itinerary depends on the goal. They are not priority on a first Egypt trip. For birds, fishing villages, Delta environment, or the ancient geography around Alexandria, they are too large to overlook on a map.

The important thing is not selling these as "hidden gems." The Delta lagoons have beautiful moments and very real problems. Value is there. Egypt's water does not only shine quietly in front of temples. It sits constantly tense between human life, industry, birds, fish, drainage, and sea-level rise.
Lakes along the Suez Canal
The Suez Canal is not only a single artificial waterway. It passes through several lakes — Lake Timsah, the Great Bitter Lake, the Little Bitter Lake.
Lake Timsah sits beside
Ismailia
. As Ismailia became an important base during canal construction, the lake became part of modern Egyptian transport and urban planning. Today it appears as a local recreation and waterside view.

The Bitter Lakes show a slightly different angle of the canal's history. When the canal connected the Red Sea and the Mediterranean, biological movement followed. Red Sea fish and invertebrates spreading into the Mediterranean through the canal is known as Lessepsian migration. The lakes are part of that route.

The Great Bitter Lake has another piece of modern history. After the 1967 war, the Suez Canal was closed and several cargo ships were trapped in the lake for a long time. The desert-dust-covered convoy was called the "Yellow Fleet," and the crews kept a community on the lake for years. A vivid case of the canal as a place wrapping military, trade, and human life together.

For travel, rather than aiming at these lakes alone, hold them in mind while moving from Cairo through Ismailia, Suez, or toward Sinai. More than the water surface, they read as part of a world transit corridor.
Lake Bardawil
On the north Sinai coast, Lake Bardawil is a shallow saltwater lake along the Mediterranean. Separated from the sea by a sandbar, it matters for fishery, salinity, birdlife, and ecology.

It deserves caution for travellers. North Sinai has long been subject to security restrictions and attention. Geographical and ecological value notwithstanding, this is not a place to recommend casually as a standard tourism stop. If you are considering a visit, confirm current security information and on-the-ground arrangements.

That point matters for Egypt's lakes generally. A place with value and a place a traveller should go to now are not the same. A body of water that looks appealing on the map can sit outside the itinerary because of security, access, environment, or protection.
Lakes a traveller can realistically see
On a first or second Egypt trip, Lake Nasser, Lake Qarun, and Wadi El Rayan are the practical choices.
Lake Nasser comes naturally into an Abu Simbel and Aswan itinerary. For depth, consider a Lake Nasser cruise.

Lake Qarun and Wadi El Rayan fit a day trip or one-night stay in Fayoum. With lakes, desert, sites, fossils, and farmland at short distances, it is a good region to see another face of Egypt without going too far from Cairo.

The Delta lagoons and the Suez Canal lakes suit specific interests. Birding, understanding the Delta environment, tracing the Suez Canal's history, reading the ancient geography around Alexandria. With those goals, the itinerary has meaning. Not for swimming, resort time, or easy scenery.
Egypt seen from the lakes
When Egypt is described, water tends to collapse into the Nile. That is not wrong. Without the Nile, Egypt does not exist.

Look at the lakes, and a slightly more complex geography appears. The place that holds Nile water. The depression that supported ancient irrigation. The new surface born of agricultural drainage. The lagoon that supports birds and fish at the boundary with the Mediterranean. The lake in the middle of the canal that connects world shipping.
Each lake shows Egypt at a slightly different angle. Not only as a backdrop for ancient civilisation — as a country that still manages water, depends on water, and is changed by water.
Lakes are not as legible as temples. They do not stay in the memory the way pyramids do. To know Egypt's real geography, don't ignore these bodies of water.
Egypt is a country of river and desert.
It is also a country of the lakes that sit on the boundary between them.

deck: A guide that reads Egypt's water and geography through Lake Nasser, Lake Qarun, Wadi El Rayan, the Delta lagoons, and the lakes along the Suez Canal.
